## Overview

The Kayapo are an Indigenous people in Brazil who live across Pará and Mato Grosso, south of the Amazon River and along the Xingu River and its tributaries. Their territory includes tropical rainforest savannah, river valleys, pools, creeks, and scattered villages ranging in population from one hundred to one thousand people. In 2018, the estimated Kayapo population was 8,638. They are one of the subgroups of the Mebêngôkre nation, a name meaning “people from the water’s source.” The Kayapo speak Mẽbêngôkre, also called Kayapo, a Northern Jê language of the Jê and Macro-Jê families. Their folk-culture significance in the sources lies in body painting, feather adornment, naming ceremonies, oral performance, shifting cultivation, traditional ecological knowledge, and continuing efforts to protect their forest territory.

## Material culture

### Textile & pattern traditions

**Body-paint designs** — Kayapó body painting uses black pigment over the body, with designs and patterns unique to each person. Red pigment is applied to the legs and rubs off on surrounding plants as people move through the forest.

**Beaded and cloth bands** — Kayapó children wear cloth or beaded bands in colors representing their tribes. These are tied below the waist or crossed around the torso.

**Feather headdresses** — Kayapó chiefs wear headdresses made from bright yellow feathers. The feathers come from birds native to their area, including the hyacinth macaw and crested oropendola, and are not dyed.

### Clothing & dress

Kayapó dress differs according to age, gender, and occasion. Older generations of Kayapó men wear wooden disks in their lower lips, although this practice is less common among younger men. Men adorn themselves with radiating feather headbands representing the universe and may wear rope in their hair, representing the rope with which the first Kayapó arrived from the sky. Traditionally, men covered the lower body with sheaths. Contemporary Kayapó often wear western-style clothing, including shorts and pants, because of increased contact with outside cultures.

Kayapó chiefs wear bright yellow feather headdresses representing the rays of the sun. Children wear cloth or beaded bands in tribal colors, and when a child comes of age, they participate in a naming ceremony during which they wear large yellow headdresses. Kayapó women can be distinguished by a “V” formation shaved into their hair.

### Architecture

Kayapó villages typically consist of a dozen huts. A centrally located hut serves as a meeting place where village men discuss community issues.

### Ceramics, metalwork & everyday objects

 They mention wooden disks worn in the lower lips, machetes carried during the Altamira demonstration, and sheaths traditionally worn by men.

### Jewelry & body adornment

Kayapó body adornment includes black body painting, red leg pigment, wooden lower-lip disks, feather headbands, feather headdresses, hair rope, and shaved hair. Kayapó people believe that their ancestors learned ways of life from insects, and body painting imitates invertebrates while helping communication with the great spirit present in all things. Black paint also helps people blend into the forest during hunting. Red pigment on the legs marks movement through vegetation. Chiefs’ yellow feather headdresses represent the rays of the sun, while men’s radiating feather headbands represent the universe. Women’s “V” hair formation is a distinguishing practice.

## Music & performance

Kayapó performance includes oratory, dances, naming ceremonies, and public demonstrations. The sources say that the Kayapo value oratory highly and call themselves *Kaben mei*, “those who speak beautifully,” in comparison with other Indigenous groups. During conflicts over hydroelectric dams, Kayapo people used traditional war oratory and dances. At the Altamira Gathering, they appeared in traditional costume and carried machetes while protesting dam development. The ProDocult documentation project recorded 150 hours of video and 15 hours of audio, alongside more than 6,000 digital photographs, documenting Kayapó language and culture.

## Dance & theatre

Kayapo dances are mentioned as part of traditional war oratory and as a means of responding to adversity during public political action. The Kayapo used dances at the Altamira Gathering, a demonstration concerning proposed hydroelectric dams in the Xingu River area.

## Festivals & rituals

 They do describe naming ceremonies and a life-cycle transition. Kayapó children participate in a naming ceremony when they come of age and wear large yellow headdresses during it. The Kayapo value beautiful names, which are understood as signs of wealth. A village may move and reconstruct its camp to find the materials needed for the ceremony, including sufficient food for the celebration, which must be gathered and presented to the newborn’s father.

The sources also describe traditional war oratory and dances used during political resistance, particularly at the Altamira Gathering.

## Foodways

A type of sweet potato or tuber is an important part of the Kayapó diet and is sometimes called “caiapo” after the tribe. The sources state that this plant is cultivated under that name in Japan and has been found to decrease insulin resistance in people with type 2 diabetes.

Kayapo agriculture uses shifting cultivation, in which land is cultivated for a few years before people move to another area and allow the old farm to lie fallow. The most frequent method is slash and burn. New fields reach peak production of principal domesticated crops in two or three years, while different crops continue reproducing for different periods: sweet potatoes for four to five years, yams and taro for five to six years, manioc for four to six years, and papaya for five or more years. The Kayapo also cultivate hidden “war gardens,” used as resources during food scarcity.

The Kayapo use approximately 250 different food plants and 650 different medicinal plants found around their villages.

## Oral tradition & literature

The Kayapo incorporate traditional myth, ritual, and cosmology into practices that honor the relationship between the earth and the people. They believe that ancestors learned ways of life from insects, a belief connected to body painting and communication with the great spirit present in all things.

Mẽbêngôkre has literary works including myth and ritual stories and descriptions of Mẽbêngôkre-speaking communities. A translation of the New Testament into Mẽbêngôkre was published in 1996. The Brazilian organization ProDocult began a documentation project on Kayapó language and culture in April 2009, producing video recordings, audio recordings, digital photographs, and films recording Mebengokre culture and its creative and dynamic character.

## Language & religion

Mẽbêngôkre, sometimes referred to as Kayapó, is a Northern Jê language within Jê and Macro-Jê. It is spoken by the Kayapó and Xikrin people in northern Mato Grosso and Pará. There were around 8,600 native speakers since 2010, according to the source’s reference to the 2015 Ethnologue 18th edition. The language has many dialects because of the number of Kayapo groups. The Kayapo language is endangered at a sixth level, and materials for literacy and education in Mẽbêngôkre are very limited.

The sources describe Kayapo traditional myth, ritual, and cosmology, including belief in a great spirit present in all things. Mẽbêngôkre uses different forms of verbs, postpositions, relational nouns, prefixes, suffixes, and case marking; it is a head-final language.
